common_name: Kent Elderberry (Early-Ripening Nova Scotia American Elderberry Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in late winter to early spring (February-April in zone 9) in moist, fertile soil; pair with Adams, York, or another cultivar for cross-pollination and heavier fruit set.

directions: Kent was selected at the Kentville Research Station in Nova Scotia from Adams-derived American elderberry stock and is best known for ripening its clusters 10-14 days ahead of Adams or York, giving growers an earlier start to the harvest window. Flat-topped cymes of small white flowers appear in late spring, followed by dense, drooping clusters of small, very sweet black berries that hold their flavor well whether used fresh-cooked, dried, or pressed into juice and syrup. In Gulf Coast heat, site Kent where afternoon shade or consistent soil moisture is available, since it was bred for a cooler maritime climate and benefits from extra irrigation during peak summer; plant it alongside a second American elderberry cultivar to ensure good pollination. Manage root suckers each season to keep the planting contained, and prune out the oldest canes in late winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Netzer performs reliably in the heat and humidity of Missouri and Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Netzer is a wild-selected Missouri ecotype of American elderberry that was carried into replicated University of Missouri and Missouri State University cultivar trials alongside Bob Gordon, Wyldewood, and Adams, where it consistently proved well adapted to hot, humid, southern-Midwest growing conditions. It bears the typical broad, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by heavy sets of small, dark purple-black berries in mid- to late summer, and its native Ozark origin gives it good tolerance of the heat and humidity that stress northern-bred cultivars. Because it grows and fruits on a similar schedule to other American elderberry selections, Netzer cross-pollinates readily with cultivars such as Adams, Bob Gordon, or Wyldewood when planted in the same bed. Cut back the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and control root suckers to prevent the planting from spreading into an unmanaged thicket.
sources: Missouri State University Center for Agroforestry
Missouri State University William H. Darr College of Agriculture

common_name: Ben Tirran Black Currant (Late-Flowering Frost-Avoiding Scottish Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Ben Tirran needs a long, cold winter chill period and is not a reliable choice for the Gulf Coast.

directions: Ben Tirran is a late-flowering, late-season release from the James Hutton Institute's black currant breeding program, bred so its blossoms open after the usual late-frost window, sharply cutting the risk of frost-damaged crops compared with earlier Ben-series currants. It forms a vigorous, compact bush carrying large, glossy black berries that ripen in late July into heavy, mechanically harvestable clusters with good resistance to powdery mildew and other common currant diseases. Because it needs a substantial cold winter chill to flower and fruit well, Ben Tirran is best suited to cold-winter regions and is unlikely to perform reliably in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens; northern growers should plant it with another black currant for cross-pollination. Harvest full clusters once berries turn glossy black and prune out about a third of the oldest wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Noir de Bourgogne Black Currant (Classic French Heirloom Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this old French cultivar needs a real winter chill and struggles in Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Noir de Bourgogne is the historic black currant of Burgundy, France, long prized as the traditional base for cassis liqueur and still regarded by many growers as the benchmark for rich, aromatic black currant flavor. It is an early-season cultivar that carries long strigs of large, intensely flavored black berries with a distinctive musky-resinous aroma, and it is self-fertile though yields improve with a second cultivar nearby. Noir de Bourgogne is quite susceptible to powdery mildew and needs a substantial number of winter chill hours to flower and fruit well, so it is a poor match for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens and is better reserved for cold-winter regions. Where it is well adapted, prune out about a third of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous, high-yielding young wood.

common_name: Perfection Red Currant (Classic American Heirloom Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Perfection needs a solid winter chill and is a marginal choice at best for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Perfection is an early-twentieth-century American red currant selection, raised from a Fay's Prolific by Cherry cross, that has stayed in commerce for over a century because of its large, long, easy-to-strip clusters of bright red, tart berries. Bushes are vigorous and self-fertile, producing heavy crops on long strigs that make hand-picking faster than on many other red currant cultivars, and the fruit is well suited to jelly, syrup, and baking as well as fresh eating once fully ripe. Like most red currants, Perfection needs a meaningful number of winter chill hours and cool summer nights to perform well, so it should be treated as an experimental, likely underperforming choice in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast plantings rather than a dependable crop. Where climate allows, keep roots cool with mulch, prune out canes older than three years each winter, and pick full clusters rather than individual berries to preserve fruit quality.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Josta is self-fertile and its thornless canes make it easier to manage than either gooseberry parent.

directions: Josta is the original jostaberry, released in 1977 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer after crossing black currant and gooseberry lines and doubling the chromosome count to stabilize a fertile hybrid; its name blends the German words for black currant (Johannisbeere) and gooseberry (Stachelbeere). Vigorous, thornless canes carry glossy, purple-black berries larger than a black currant but smaller than a gooseberry, with a mild, sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating, jam, and juice, and the plant shows strong natural resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf-spot diseases that trouble many gooseberries. Josta is more heat-tolerant than most true black currants, though it still fruits best with reliably moist soil and some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers. Prune out the oldest third of canes each dormant season to keep the naturally spreading, arching bush productive and open to light and air.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; pair Jogranda with Jostine or another jostaberry cultivar for best cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Jogranda was released in 1985 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer as a follow-up to the original Josta jostaberry, selected for violet-black berries that run noticeably larger than Josta's and ripen two to three weeks later, which stretches the jostaberry picking season into midsummer. The spreading, slightly drooping canes benefit from light staking or a simple wire support as the heavy fruit clusters develop, and the thornless growth habit keeps harvest and pruning far less prickly than picking true gooseberries. Flavor is tangy and full-bodied, closer to black currant than gooseberry, and the fruit holds up well for jam, syrup, and home winemaking. Jogranda crops most heavily when planted with Jostine or another jostaberry for cross-pollination, and like other jostaberries it tolerates Gulf Coast heat better than straight black currants provided it gets consistent moisture and some afternoon shade.
